result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.strong_product()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Compute the strong product of this graph with another. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.strong_product()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Compute the strong product of this graph with another. title: >- [Graph.strong_product()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Compute the strong product of this graph with another. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute the strong product of this graph with another. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L39826-L39879){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.strong_product(other) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Strong product](/assets/graphs/strong-product.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="G is a path a–b–c (accent edges) and H a path 1–2–3 (teal). Their strong product is the 3 by 3 king's graph, labeled a1 to c3: accent edges along the rows copy G, teal edges down the columns copy H, and ink diagonals move both coordinates at once. It has 9 nodes and 20 edges, and the center (b, 2), outlined, reaches all 8 others." width="100%"} The strong product $G \boxtimes H$ is the union of the Cartesian and tensor products: `(g, h)` and `(g', h')` are joined when each coordinate either stays put or moves along an edge, and at least one moves. A path times a path is a grid with its diagonals, the "king's graph" of chess, so the strong product models moves that may change several coordinates at once, and its graph distance is the maximum (Chebyshev) of the factor distances. It appears in information theory: the Shannon capacity of a channel is defined through strong powers of its confusability graph. Both graphs must be directed or both undirected. Edges from the Cartesian part keep the weight and attributes of their factor edge; edges from the tensor part get the product of the two weights. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [other]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The second factor. Neither graph is modified. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph with `n * m` nodes, numbered and labeled as in `cartesian_product()`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If one graph is directed and the other is not. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The product has $n|E_H| + m|E_G| + 2|E_G||E_H|$ edges when undirected and simple, and $d((g, h), (g', h')) = \max(d_G(g, g'), d_H(h, h'))$. When both factors are simple the product is simple, matching NetworkX's `strong_product`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A 3 x 3 king's graph: the center square reaches all 8 others in one move: ::: {#0ce332e5 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec p3 = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["a", "b", "c"]).add_edges([("a", "b"), ("b", "c")]) p3_ranks = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["1", "2", "3"]).add_edges([("1", "2"), ("2", "3")]) kings = p3.strong_product(p3_ranks) kings.count_edges(), kings.get_degree("(b, 2)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (20, 8) ``` ::: :::
